BOMBARDMENT OF TANG I Kit. Wo need scarcely inform our readers that the French do not occupy Morocco, neither will they be allowed to do so. Front the Morning Chronicle we copy the following extract of a letter, written by a gentleman who accompanied Mr. Ilitv, on his mission to the Emperor. The facts con tained in this tetter are very important, and increase our regret at the unexpected step taken by the þÿi rince de Joinville. þÿ You (rtay, perhaps, he already aware that 1 accompanied Mr. Diummond Hay in his embassy to the Sultan of Morocco. Alter remaining 17 days at Morocco, we left it on the 29th ult., with every hope that the mission had succeeded, and on the 5dt of August we had a personal interview with the Sultan at Rabat. He received us with the greatest kindness, seemed rcallv grateful It Mr. þÿHay s interference in the French and Spanish u Hit its, and ended by conceding tw.ru point in question, bill by I1 nine e and Spain. We were, therefore, surprised to hear a heavy cannonade next morning, when about 15 miles from Tangier, and on coming into the bav about eleven þÿo clock, found the Pi nice de J linville, with dime line of battle ships, a frigate, two brigs, and nine steamers, bombarding the town. Besides the English ships Altiion, Warspite. and Hecla. there were also in the bay the Spanish squadron, and an American, a Swedish, a Sardinian, and a Danish frigate and a Danish steamer. On the night of the 5th the Prince uxis on board the Alt)ion, stated his intention of leav-

ing for Cadiz, and hoped that all u-ould be permanently settled i but declared that he knew nothing whatever ol Hay 's mission, and that if necessary to proceed to hostilities, he could not wail for his return. flie French fired very boldly. They began the allair with three broadsides. '1 hey tune 20 men killed and wounded, and the IS nil re n has <0 shot m her hull. 1 he Moors fought very gallantly. After six hours' firing, the Fionch ships were lowed oil by their steamers, the forts firing on them, and not a Hag struck. 1 was on shore at Tangier yes terdav. The town is scarcely damaged at all, the defences about the water port a good deal, but no breach anywhere. The Moors had one man killed, and one wounded (since dead',; two children lolled by fall of a bouse. There are but 300 regular soldiers in the town, and they have defended it faithfully against the Kabyles. who are in great num- þÿ bers outside, and wish to pillage and burn it 'The. following is a copy ot a letter from a French officer engaged m the bombardment. This document, which is characterised by an air of l rui! dullness, gives the only intelligible account of the reasons which induced the prince do Joinville so unexpectedly to depart liom the pacific intentions expressed by him the 5 ill when on hoard - þÿ the Albion on the evening ol . Ta.nuibk Roads, Aug 7. þÿ The bombardment of 'Tangier took us all by surprne; so much so, that on the afternoon of the oth preparations were made to return to Cadiz Falcon the same evening the Prince receiv-
ed dispatches liom Paris, ordering him to get possession of Dingier and Mogador and within an hour afterwards other dispatches were received from Marshal Huge and, stating

3 T þÿ tilit ¬ 'll A T 'I 3 . in clear terms that the conduct of the Emperor was most treacherous, and that the only object hi negociating was to gain time. J he Prince immediately assembled a council of war and ihe next morning at break ol day all was in movement. At half past eight a. m., ilie Suliren and Gemappes, having been laid along the town, opened a tremendous fire, amidst the most deafening cries of Vive le þÿHoi, Vive le Prince de Joinville þÿ 'The enemy received us with great sangfroid, and for the first hour stood well to their guns, but we were too much for them, and at 25 minutes past ten all the fortifications were knocked down, i doubt much that we have put many of the enemy, hors de combat ; they were well protected bv covered ways, and we dearly saw that about nine þÿo clock they had m a great measure abandoned the forts. 1 know not whether the town has suffered much. I should suppose it had, lor the Rubis showered about 50 congreve rockets, the greater pail of which fell on that part ol the city inhabited by the natives. VV hilsi we were attacking the forts, one ot the þÿenemy s batteries placed at one of the extremities took us sideways, and greatly incommoded us, but tlie Triton and Belie þÿl oule, having placed themselves opposite this battery, soon destiny ed it Another buttery on the shoie, mounted by four pieces ot 80, was soon silenced by the Cussard. We had much to contend with, for the wind was against us, and a heavy sea caused our vessel to roll most tremendously. 1 he conduct of our

voung commander was most aurnrrable ; lie never for a moment quitted the deck of the Sutlicn; his orders were given wait great coolness, he animated the sailors, and took Ins station at the post of honour, vvhete there was the most danger. During the action the English and foreign vessels kept a strict neutrality and watched every movement of the Prince. Our loss is insignificant ; about two or three killed, and about tinny wounded. 'To morrow we leave for Mogador ; and, alter giving tlie enemy oilier lessons there, and at Sane and Earache, we return to Cadiz, and thence to Madeira to take m provisions. A person who escaped from the town and sought refuge on board the Gemappes, gives as positive dial tlie Emperor has ordered a levee en masse, and that the Holy War is being preached throughout die kingdom."

HISTORICAL NOTICES OF TAN- GIER. Tangier is situated near the western entrance to the Straits of Gibraltar, built at the entrance of a bay, on the side of a hill overlooking the sea, and about fourteen miles west of Gape Spartak It has a population of 1)000 souls; and, in conjunction with Tetuan, supplies Gibraltar, Cadiz, Lisbon, and other ports on the coast of Spain and Portugal, with fowls, beef, mutton, and fruit. Dining the memorable siege ot Gibralter, 1779 82, Tangier was of considerable importance to tlie English, from whence much valuable information respecting tlie move merits of the French and Spaniards was constantly transmitted. It may not, however, fie generally known þÿ that Tangier was formerly in the possession of the English, having been ceded by þÿi ortu <-a|, in 1003, to King Charles the Second on the occasion of bis marriage with Donna Cntherina, infanta of Portugal, as j ai t of her dowry, in the spring ol 1080 Tangier was

þÿ - - »| besieged by an army from Morocco, and Charles recommended tlie parliament to take measures for its preservation. 'I fie occupa. lion of Tangier was said to be of importance to the Levant trade, and it was feared that two millions embarked in that cummer o would be lost. Consequently, detect met is from each of the three troops of Life Cu.m1-, 260 officers and men from tlie first þÿI t Guards; and 130 officers and men (torn tlie Coldstream Guards, under the command of the Earl of Mulgravc, were dispatched to garrison tlie fortress of Tangier, and on their arrival were st\ led 'The þÿKing s battalion. þÿ These were followed by the Earl of I urnþÿbarton s regiment (now the 1st, or Royal Regiment), and the Eail of þÿInrhiqnin s (now the 2d, or þÿQueen s Royals) Mm h tigiuu g took place between the Moors and the Eng lisli with varied success, and langiet was closely besieged by tiie barbarians On the 2'itii September, 1080, a general sadv < I tie garrison was made on the Moorish lilies, where 15.000 troops were encamped. '1 tie action soon became general, and þÿDumbarton s renowned veterans quickly cairied the redoubts, although with immense saughter; the Guards and tlie Queen's Royals equally suffered, for the returns give an aggirgate loss of 1 1 officers and 100 men killed, and 34 officers and 334 men wounded. King Charles II. found ihe maintenance of a sufficient garrison at Tangier to be too expensive; and the nation refusing to grant supplies, the fortifications and mole were

Extraordinary Phenomenon. þÿ Several German journals give an account of an extraordinary phenomenon which took place a short time since in the lake near the convent of Each. While the weather was perfectly serene, the waters of the lake rose in a few minutes, and overflow7 the banks on all sides I hey alter a short space again subsided, and retired to a point far lower than their original level, exposing several extensive abysses which had been hitherto unknown. A loud subterraneous noise was at the same time heard ; the trees on the banks were torn up by the roots, and large crevices formed in the banks. A sulphureous vapour arose, and a great Humber of fish were observed to float dead on the surface of the water. Many birds were also suffocated by the odour.

On the 9th. between 9 and 1 1 o'clock m ihe night, nnlv 17 of these falling stars wore ohsei ved ; but on the 10th (the regular period of their return) Dr. Forster found that the number of those which crossed the western hemisphere alone amounted to rather more than 70 per hour. Sonic were exceedingly brilliant, and variously coloured, whilst others left long trains of light in their track. VV fiat was most remarkable, was their evident tendency to a converging point in the heavens, very near to Antares, in the heait ol the Scorpion. Indeed, hardly any exceptions appeared to this rule; and yet they commenced from every quarter, a circumstance that will be very interesting to astronomers i:i distant paits. One of the most brilliant of these meteors appeared at 35 minutes past 10, mean time at Bruges, and it crossed the zenith, or nearly so, not far from tiie first star of the Harp, descending towards the horizon in a direction WSW. Besides the ordinary meteors, Dr. Forster observed some remarkable white lines, apparently electric, which seemed as if drawn along the sky, momentarily, and which hud also a direction towards WfSW. Obseneis will now wait anxiously fur ttie 12th and 13:h of November, which is the next period of the meteors. þÿ Galignani.

The Chinese mode of taking wild fowl, with which the neighbourhood of Canton abounds, is curious and somewhat unsportmanlike. þÿ 1 here is no missing fire no powder getting þÿ damp þÿ no barrels þÿbursting no bother with dogs þÿ nothing but sport. Whenever they see a quantity of ducks settled in any particular piece of water they send half a dozen gourds to float among them. These gourds resemble the pumpkins in England ; but being hollowed out, they float on the surface of the water. On large pools they leave from 20 to 00 afloat. At first the fowl are shy at coming near them, but by degrees they get courage, and as all birds at length grow familiar with a scare crow, they soon gather round them, and amuse themselves bv whetting their bills against them. When the birds get pretty familiar with them the sportsmen prepare to deceive them more effectually. þÿ A Chinese hollows out a pumpkin which is pretty large, and after making Ivies to see and breathe through, he claps n on his head. Thus accoutred he wades slowly into the water, keeping his body under, and letting nothing be seen above the surface but the pumpkin in vvhis.h is his head. In this manner he moves imperceptibly towards the fowls, which suspect no danger. At last he fairly gets in amongst them; while thev, having been long used to see gourds, take not the ieast alarm, even when the enemy is in the very midst of them ; who Whenever he approaches a fowl, seizes it bv the þÿlegs and nese, draws it with a jerk under the water. He
then fastens it to his girdle and proceeds on to the next victim, till lie has loaded himself with as many as he can walk off with.-- Pidding's Chinese Olio.

Origin of the French National Guards. þÿ Talleyrand was fond of telling a story apropos of Sieves, illustrative of the theory of great results from little causes. He was one day walking with him through the Tuileries, when, just opposite the gate in the Place de la Concorde, a little beggar girl, leading an old woman on crutches, came up to solicit aims. Sieves gave her a sou, which in her hurry to seize she let fall, and the coin rolled under the hoofs of the charger mounted by the garde da corps on duty at the gate. The child pressed forward to pick it up, but each time that she stooped, almost at the risk of her life, the soldier, apparently

glad to divert the ennm of sentry by an event ol litis kind, spurred the animal to one side, and the wretched little girl, to avoid being crushed to death, was compelled to withdraw to renew again her endeavours þÿa soon as the beast stood still, but each lime with as little success as before. The whole scene þÿ the terror of the child þÿ the overboiling wrath of the old cripple, and the insolent and cruel mirth of the garde du corps, presented altogether a most exciting spectacle, and combined with the angry passions of the crowd, who were not slow to take the part of the child, formed a picture not easily forgotten. Sieves, finding that the people were growing angry, thought it best to put an end to the scene at once, so giving the girl a double sou he bade her begone, which, injunction she immediately obeyed, and the crowd forthwith dispersed. But Sieves remained thoughtful during the whole evening, and when he parted with his friend lie said, I have been thinking over the occurrence we witnessed together this morning. Something must he done for the people. When they have an army of their own they w ill not run the risk of being insulted bv hired þÿmercenaries. This was the very fiisi idea which had ever entered human brain respecting the formation ot a national guard. Once started, the idea found favour with all the disatlected. Sieves himself planned and invented the projet. and, by dint of perseverance, got it accepted some long time alterþÿW ard3. Little did the proud Garde Nation -

ale, when they marched to the frontier þÿ when they dictated laws to the þÿcountry when they barricaded Fans þÿ dream that they owed their existence and creation to a halfpenny which a starving beggar wench found hard to pick out of the guttei þÿ! The Talleyrand Papers.

So many friends, so many joys, desert us during our pilgrimage through þÿlife the sun remains true to us, and lights and warms us from the erad'e to the grave. The highest fes'ival of the year among the Northern Heathens and Christians occurs also at the season in which the sun, as it were, is born anew to the earth, and his strength is converted from waning to waxing. licent meal : even the poorest dnv laborer, if he himsell possesses no corn, asks and receives from t fie peasants a bundle of corn, raises it aloft, and makes the birds rejoice beside Ins empty barn. þÿ Miss Lremer.

þÿ ' - . -- .. i ' LIFE, DEATH, AND THE FUTURE. In a few short years we learn that the þÿ valley of the shadow of þÿdeath does but lead to a place ol peace, þÿ where the wicked cease from troubling, and the weary are at þÿrest. Rest! þÿ how strongly, day by day, does the desire for rest grow upon the human heart! We begin life þÿ how buoyant, how hopeful ! difficulties but bring out a heathfui exertion, and obstacles stimulate by the resources they call into action. This cannot and does not last; it is not lassitude so much as discouragement that gains upon os; we feel how little we have done of all we once thought that we could do; and still more, how little that we have done has answered us intention. This 1 believe to be experienced in every career ; hut more especially in a literary one. Necessarily dependent on imagination, feeling, and opinion, of how exhausting a nature is both the woik and the appeal of literature ! Let the successful writer look hack a few years, and what an utter sense of desolation there will he in the retrospect ! Not a volume but has been the burial place of many hopes, and the graven record of feelings never to he known again. How constantly has mortification accompanied triumph ! With what secret sorrow has that praise been received from strangers, denied to us by our friends ! Nothing astnn ishes me more than the envy which attends literary fame, and the unkindly depreciation which waits upon the writer : of every species of fame, it is the most ideal and apart ; it

would seem to interfere with no one. It is bought by a life of labor ; generally, also, of seclusion and privation. What hours of feverish misery have been past I What bit ter tears have been shed over the unjust censure, and the personal sarcasm. The imaginative feel such wrong far beyond what those of less sensative temperament enn dream. The very essence of a poetical mind is irritable, passionate, and yet tender, susceptible, and keenly alive to that opinion which is the element of its existence. These may tie faults; hut they are faults by which themselves suffer most, and without which they could not produce their creations- Cau you bid the leopard leave his spots, and yet be beautiful ? Perhaps þÿ for the divine purpose runs through every aim of our being þÿ the disap' pointment and the endurance are but sent to raise those hopes above, which else might cling too fondly to their fruition below. Sooner or later dawns upon us the conviction, that the gifts we hold most glorious were given for a higher object than personal enjoyment, or the praise which is of man. We learn to look at the future result, to acknowledge our moral responsibility, and to hope that our þÿthoughts destined , to become part of the human mind, will worthily fulfill the lofty duty assigned to their exercise. Worn, weary, and discouraged, the image of death seems like a pleasant sleep þÿ solemn, hut soothing ; when all that now makes the fevered heart heat with unquiet pain will he no more. But I, also, gaze beyond, in all tfie

mind is imperishable ; and is also the worthiest offerings to the Creator. Whatever of thought, of feeling, or of faculties, 1 may ever have possessed look to the grave as to rfla altar, from whence they will arise purified and exalted unto heaven.

To lo v 15 On k and Wri> Another þÿ He loved one, and was wed to another. Earth has no such misery. It is wretchedness to pine through long years of uncertain absence subjected to all the casualties of doubt and distance, feeding on long expectation : till, as the scripture so touchingly says, hope deferred is sickness to the heart : still tlieie is hope, and lore has a store of subtle happiness in the many links that memory delights to bind, and whose tender recallings are the dearest guarantee for the future.

It is wretchedness to kneel by the grave of the departed, who have taken with them the verdure from the sky ; who have left home and heart alike desolate : but then the soul assorts its diviner portion, looks afar oil through the valley of the shadow of teais, and is intensely conscious that here is but atrial and beyond is its triumph. The love that dwells with the dead has a sanctity in its sorrow ; for love, above all things, asserts that vve are immortal, lint wretchedness takes no form, varied as ate its m nv modes iu this ,»ur weary existence, Itke that where the hand is given, and the heart is far away where the love vowed at the altar is not that which lies crushed, yet not quenchedt within the hidden soul Hope brings no com fort ; for there weic cruelty and crime in Us promises: memory has no solace; it can, at best, onlv crave þÿoblivion- and oblivion of what? Of all life's sweet dreams, and deepest feelings. Yet what slight things must, with a sting like 1 hat of the adder, bring hack the past þÿ too dear, and yet too bitter! a word, a look, a tone, may be enough to wring everv puise with the agony of a vain and forbidden regret.

The Love of Latch Life þÿ Must the beauty of love and worth of life be at an end to woman when her first spring, tier bloom of love, her moments of romance are past? No. do not believe that Nothing in this world is such an illusion as this belief Life is rich ; its tree blossoms eternally, because it is nourished by immortal color and glory, but all beautiful ; let us undervalue none of them, for all of them are capable of producing plants of eternal life. Youthful love þÿ the beaming passion flower of earth ! Who will belie its captivating beauty, who will not thank the Creator that he gave it to the children of earth? But ah I I will exclaim to ali those who drink of its nectar, rind to those who must do without it. There are flowers which are as noble as this, and which ate less in danger than it of being paled by the frosts of the þÿearth flowers from whose chalices also you may suck life from the life of the Eternal þÿI

Ah ! if we only understood how near to us Providence has placed the fountains of our happiness þÿ if we had only understood this from t lie days of our childhood upwards, acted upon it, and profiled by it, our lives would then seldom lead through dry wilderness! Happy are those children whose eyes are eurlv opened by parents and home to the rich activity of life. They will then experience what sweetness and joy' and peace can flow out of family relation-ships, out of the heart fell union between brothers and sisters, between parents and children; and they will experience how those relations, carefully cherished, in youth, will become blessings lor our maiurer years.

The great improvement in the time part consists principally in the escapement, which may be called a trictionless escapement ; and in the regulating motion, which may be called a rotary or torsion pendulum. The hall is tuur and a half inches in diameter þÿ of a globular form and hollow, and suspended by a steel spring ; near the upper end of the spring is an arm in the form of a crank ; the revolvtrig ot the ball twists the spring, and causes t Be arm to perform an arc, acting upon and teceiving the impulse from the swing wheel by means of a lever connected with the arm arid the pallets or escapement; which impulse is carried through the spring to the Fall, and keeps it in motion. The spring in a quiescent slate is longest; by its bein» twisted either way from that state is shortened and the hall made to rise, returning by ihe te action of the spring, and llie force rrf gravity receiving the impulse from the maintaining power at each return, I he advantages these possess over the common clock or time piece, are That very little care is required in setting it up, in consequence of its not being so liable to he put out ot heat, as other clocks They require no oil on the pallets or teeth ot the swing wheel, tlieie being no friction

between them, and the number of the revolutions of the swing wheel are sixty times less, or in other words is sixty years in making as many revolutions as the thirty nine inch or second pendulum clock does in one year þÿ And it requires moie than fifty times less maintaining power; consequently a very large amount less of friction and wear, than in other clocks, and therefore the motion much more regular. REPOllT OF MARSHAL RVGEAUD, Camp, near Condiat Abderrahman, ) Aug. 17. ) " AT. le Marechal þÿ Tiie son of the Emperor, Mulev Abderrahman. not having made reply to the letter I wrote to him alter the sort of summons tie addressed to me to evacuate Lalla Migrania, if we were anxious for peace, his army daily received fresh reinforcements, and his pride increased with his forces. The Moors openly spoke in tiis camp of taking Tlemceii, (Iran, M tscara, and even Algiers. It was a real crusade to retrieve the affairs of Islamism. They thought thai we could not resist so large a body of the most renowned horsemen in the empire of Morocco, and they were onlv waiting to attack us for the arrival of the contingents of infantry of the Beni Senassen and Bif, who were to assail us from the mountains, at the foot of which stands the camp of I. alia Magrania, whilst an iinin mse cavalry would surround us on the side of the plain. " The nine days of uncertainty which had just elapsed had already alarmed the minds uf the natives in my rear ; hostile parties, had already twice attack d our envoys of Ifjemmn Ghar. out, and the good will of the tribes of which I he v consisted was near giving way. Two reconnoitring parties came to within the distance of a pistol shot of I, alia Magrania, and attacked our out posts. A long doubt as to our force, and as to our wish to fight the adversaries whom we had in front, might have provoked revolts behind us, and, besides other embarrassments, might

have stopped the victualling of the army of the west. I should have preferred, from the excessive heat, to have waited for the attack than to have gone to attack an imemv whi h was at a distance of eight hours from me; but the dangers of waiting any longer made me decide upon taking the initiative. "General Bed' au having joined me on the 12th witli three battalions and six squadrons, I advanced on the fifth, at three p. n þÿ feigning to make a grand forage, in order not to let the enemy understand that it really was an offensive movement. At nightfall the foiagers returned towards the columns, and we encamped in matching order in silence, and without lighting fires. At two in the morning I was again in movement. 1 passed a first time i fie Isly, at dawn, without meeting the enemv. On arriving, at eight o'clock in the morning, on the heights of Djurfel- Akhdar, we perceived all the Moorish camps stilt in their places, extending over the slopes of the rigiit bank. All the cavalry composing them had moved forward, in order to attain us at the second passage of the liver. Amidst a large mass stationed on tfie highest part, we perfectly distinguished the gioup of tile Emperor's soil, his flags and his parasol þÿ the badge of bis command It was the point I gave to the battalion of direction of tnv echelmini order, (hi ai living thither, we were to move to the right and march to the camps, wlnl.it keeping the summit ot the fulls with the letl face of mv square of squares. þÿ All the leaders of the several parts of my
order of combat were near me ; I rapidly gave the Hi my instructions, ami after a huh

>sV T, Mtrix ATJ8. of five or six minutes, we descended to the fords, at the mere 'pas wealth,' and to the sound of the instruments "Numerous horse defended the passage; they were repulsed by my infantry tirailleurs, with some loss on both sides, and 1 soon reached the plateau immediately below the highest spot where the Emperoi's son stood. 1 directed upon it the tire of my four fieldpieces, and the utmost confusion was forthwith manifested. At this moment enoinuius masses of cavalry issued on both sides from the back of the lull, A, assailed at i tie same lime my two flanks and my rear it i< quired all the solidity of my infantry ; not a man betrayed any weakness. Our tirailleurs, wtio were at only 50 paces ft urn tne squares, him ly awaited the multitude, without reining a single step; they had otders to lie down if the charge extended to them, m oiuer not to obstruct the fire of the squares. Upon the lints of the dead angles of the batiuiieiiis tire artillery poured grape shot. " 1 tie enemy's masses were stopped, and began to turn about. 1 acceleiated their retreat, and increased their confusion, by directing against them my four held pieces which marched at the head of the column þÿ As soon as 1 saw that the enemy's efforts against my flanks were broken, I continued my match onwards. The enemy's cavalry being divided by us own movements, and by my march, which cut it in two, 1 deemed i tie moment come to make mine issue upon ibe capital point, which, in my opinion, was the camp 1 supposed to be attended by the in-

fantry and artillery. 1 ordered Colonel Tartas to echelonner bis lit squad ions by the left, so that his last echelon might icst on the right bank of the Isly. "Colonel J usuf commanded the first echelon, which consisted of six squadrons of Spahis, very closely supported in the tear by three squadrons of the 4ih Chasseuts. Having put to the sword a good number of horse, Colonel Jusuf attacked that immense camp, alter receiving several discharges of artillery : he found it filled with horse and foot soldiers, w ho disputed every inch of the ground. The reserve of the three squadrons of t fie 4th Chasseurs arrived a fresh impulse þÿ was imparted the artillery was captuied and the þÿ þÿ camp carried. It was covered with dead bodies and dead horses. The w h de artillery, all the provisions and war stores, the tent of the Emperor's son, the tents of all the ciiiefs, the shops of numerous traders accompanying the army, everything, in short, remained in one power. But this biiynt episode of the campaign cost us dear þÿ four officers of tfie Spnhis and Chasseurs had lost their lives in it, several others were wounded. Meanwhile Colonel Morris, who commanded the 2d and 3d echelons, seeing a large mass of cavalry rushing again on my right wing, passed the Isly in older to break that charge by attacking the enriny on their right flank. The attack upon our infantry failed like the others; but Colonel Morris had to sustain the most unequal combat. Unable to retire without exposing himself to a defeat, be resolved on

energetically combating until succoured. þÿ This struggle lasted about hall an hour ; those six squadrons were succcssivi ly and repeatedly engaged ; our Chasseurs achieved piodtgies of valour ; 300 horse, Berbers or Abids Bokhari, fell under their blows. " At last. General Bedcau, commanding the right wing, seeing tfie immense danger the 2d Chasseurs was exposed to, detached

the battalion of Zouaves, a battalion of t lie 15th Light Infantry, and the 9th battalion of Chasseurs of Oilcans, in order to attack the enemy on the side ot the mountains That movement determined their retreat. Colonel Morris then resumed the offensive against them, and executed several successful charges in the pass by which they were retiring ; that episode was one of the most vigorous of tfie day, 550 Chasseurs of the 2d combated 0000 of the enemy's cavalry. " The infantry fiat! not been long in following to tfie camp the first echelon of eavah v ; the enemy had rallied in a large mass on the left bank ol t lie Isly, and seemed to piepuie to recapture the camp; the intiniry anil artillery rapidly crossed it, the artillery placed itself in battery on the right hank, and discharged grape shot on that vast confusion of horse, assembling from all sides. ing to the mountains of the Beni -Sennssen. - It was then noon, the heat was great, the trooj s of i. ed in turn by from three to four thousand cavalry at a lime, and nothing confused them even for a moment The artillery went in front of the squares to throw their grapeshot to greater advantage ; the cavalry, when the proper moment came, advanced with an irresistible impetuosity and overthrew everything it found in front of it.

'The St. I.ouis Era snvs : þÿ " Spanish quarters are not received in Bank, they are refused at the l'ost Office, will not pass in the Land Office, and we observe that auctioneers now give notice thai they will not be received by them at par. Our own decimal coins are much more convenient. Until we can obtain a sufficiency of American coin for circulation we must use what we can procure in the market II is bad policy in Banks and Post Offices or any other t ublic institution to refuse Spanish coin at its current value. A Hare Tight. þÿ - On Easter Sunday afternoon, as 1 was proceeding with my brother in-law, Mr Can. to look at a wild duck's nest in an adjacent wood, we saw two hares fighting with inconceivable fury on the open ground, about a hundred and till v yards distant from us. They stood on their hinder legs like two bull dogs resolutely bent on destruction. Having watched them for about a quarter of an hour, we then entered the wood ; i observing to Mr. Carr that we should find them engaged on our return. We staid in the wood ten minutes, and on leaving it, we saw the hares siill in desperate battle. They had moved along the hill side, and the grass was strongly marked with their down for a space of twenty yards. At last 'one of the sylvan warriors fell on its side, and never got upon its legs again. Its antagonist then retreated for a yard or so,- stood still for a minute, as if in contemplation, and then tushcd vergefully on the fallen foe. This retreat and advance was perfumed many tines; þÿ the conqueror striking his prostiale adversary with its fore feet, and clearing off great quantities of down with them. In the mean lime the vanquished hate rolled over and over again, hut cou'd not recover the use of its legs, although it made several attempts to do so. lis movements put you in mind of a drunken man trying to get up from the floor after a hard night in the aie house. It now lay still on the ground, effectually subdued ; whilst the other continued its attacks upon il, with the fury of a little demon. Seeing that

the fight was over, we approached the scene of action. þÿ the conqueror hare retiring as we drew near. 1 took up the fallen combatant just as it w as hreathingits last. Both its sides had been completely bared of fur, and large patches of down had been torn front its Tack and belly. It was a well conditioned buck hare, weighing, I should suppose, some seven or eight pounds. Mr. Carr's groom was standing by the stable door, as 1 came up, with the hare in my hand. Here, John, said 1, take this to your own house, and get Hour wife to dress it lor your family ; it is none the worse for being killed on Easter Sunday: þÿ arid then I told him how it had come into my possession He thanked me kindly for it ; and 1 learnt from Mr. Carr at the end of the week, that John's wife had made it into a pie, with the addition of a few rashers of bacon; that it proved to he uncommonly good; þÿ and that they would all remember, for many venrs to come, the fight betwixt the two baits in the park at Walton Hail, on Easter Sun- " day afternoon, the 10;h of April 1843

From Bell's Weekly Messenger , London September QU. 1844. FoitEtoM 1tci,uoi:nce France and þÿ þÿMorocco Two official reports have been published during the week, confirming the happy intelligence of the final ratification of the preliminaries of pence between France and Morocco. The first was a telegraphic dispatch from the þÿI rince de Juinville to the government, announcing that the Governor ol Tangiers had visited his vessel immediately upon his arrival : that the conditions of peace Were then signified to him, and accepted, and signed on the spot. This satisfactory intelligence has since been fully confirmed by official dispatches to our own government 1rom Mr, Bulwer, her þÿMajesty s minister at Madrid, dated the 1 1 th September, and received in London on Wednesday the 18th. þÿ The terms of the treaty ate the same in substance as those originally offered. Thus this peril is over ; indeed we never entertained any misgiving upon the subject, and our readers will do us the justice to n member that we laboured earnestly and zealously to dispel the public panic. Indeed, we begin to entertain most sanguine expectations that none of us, who are now in middle age, will live to see another war of any extent or duration. The long French wars ha«e produced this happy change in the governments and people of Flu rope They have taught them the sure misery of national warfare; the peril of them to kings, and the pressure and exhaustion <>f them upon the people, in the shape of high taxes, and the destruction of commerce. Hence one happy change in the

character of the age: it is now a first principle with all the governments of Europe to employ their common efforts in mediating in those incidental jars and collisions which occur between any two of their neighbours, and thus employing the influence of their own power and authority in the pacific settlement of such differences. The French people, always restless and too much inclined for war, are tints restrained by the wholesome sobriety of the well-understood power of Great Britain, who is cordially supported by the co operation of Austria. The Emperor of Russia, another warlike power, is also kept !u check by tue same salutary influence of England, Austria, and l'russia. Under this state of tilings we have no apprehension of any interruption of the geneial peace. It would, indeed, be a strange departure from common sense, if the two pitiful affairs of Morocco and Otalieite had been permitted to disturb the geneial repose of Europe. !n conclusion of the affairs of France, it is only necessary to add that the happy issue o the negociatioiis relating to Morocco and Otalieite has confirmed M. Guizot in his administration. and has broken the power of the extraordinary confederacy of French Conservatives and Radicals against his ministry. þÿI aris is now a scene of gaiety and contentment : the King has become again popular and every second nr third day is made a holiday or fate. The French colonies are also flourishing, and the contest between the growers of beet root sugar and the colonial

planters lias been amicably and satisfactorily settled. Sr mn. þÿ In Spain, if we except the province of "Navarre, where the Garlists threaten to give the government some trouble, affairs arc also proceeding in a course of prosperity which was little anticipated. Geneial Nar-

$ 1H V 'J &T1 3 vaez, in order to make adherents and prop up his own personal power, adopted the Conservative party, and induced the Queen to stop the plunder of the Spanish church, and to support the landed ami the ngricultuial interests; to publish an amnesty of all past offences; to reduce the expenditure of government, and to maintain domestic manufactures. The result has been that a large majority of Conservative members have been returned to the new chambers, and that the Spanish Radicals no longer possess the power of disturbing the peace of the country by republican laws and the subversion of establishments. It is another curious feature in Spanish affairs, that justice is remiuied to die real merits of Espnrtero ; his moderation is now universally praised, and we should not be surprised of his recal into Spain should speedily follow ; not indeed as a minister, but as one of those generals upon whonr. the Q ueen and kingdom can depend. þÿ Ibid

This Danger of Wet Clothes. þÿ Evaporation always produces cold, because the heat which is required to convert water intoxicant must tie withdrawn from the surrounding medium ; hence wet summers art often sueneeded by cold winters, the greater evaporation produced from the excessive moisture having reduced tiie temperature of the earth. That evaporation produces cold may be

immediately pioved by moistening the palm ol the hand and expo, si ,g ,t to the wind, ti us causing evaporation, when cold will be v< ry sensibly felt, and the more so it we use a volatile Hind, such as sal volatile or spirit of wine, the greater rapidity with which they evaporate producing a greater degiee of cold. It is from this reason that remaining in wet clothes is so dangerous; the evaporalion that takes place during the time they are drying, carries away so large a portion ol itcat from tiic body, as almost certain to induce cold. When a person is obliged to remain in wet clothes, the best method to adopt is to prevent evaporation bv covering them w ith a macintosh, or any oilier garment, which will best keep the moisture in ; and if this be effectually done, the person will feel little inconvenience from ins damp cloihes ; the warmth of the body will soon communicate itself to the damp garments under the macintosh, and as the steam cannot escape through it, there is nothing to j roduce a greater degree ot cold than if the garments had been dry.

Amidst the various ties which unite society together, and become antidotes to the pains and misfortunes of life, none ought to be considered so completely binding, as those which exist between the parent and the child. I he heart that is alive to grateful emotions, must continually be reverting to the kindness it has received ; yet memory cannot extend to a recollection of those anxieties, which, during the days of childhood, the attached patent feels. That there have been monsters in existence, whose depravity of disposition have absolutely brought human nature into disgrace þÿ the historian's pen too fully authenticates ; and to make it the more shocking, even in the softer race ! With what horror do we turn from the description of that parricide, who instigated her husband to deprive her aged father of his throne: and not only beheld bis venerable form mangled by his inhumane murderers, but absolutely drove over it with her chariot wheels ! Amidst all the horrors of the T rench revolution, it opened a field for the exertion of some ol the liuest feelings ol the heart: and during that fatal period, filial fondness in particular, was carried to a degree of enthusiasm that was never before displayed. Numerous are the instances of amiable daugh ters, anxious to purchase existence for the authors of their beings, by a resignation of

their own ; and even the savage multitude, who delighted in bloodshed, hav.; hen awed into compassion by ihe proof of filial love þÿ M Du llroca's interesting Anecdotes abound with instances of affection, which at once pa u and delight: and the one which J shall seiect for the entertainment of my reader-, will prove, that filial tenderness is capable of in. spiring magnanimity in the mind. Mademoiselle Cazotte was ifte only daugbter of a gentleman who, at the commencement of the revolution, was seventy tuo years ol age ; and being closely conn- cttd with the intendarit of the civil list, was ft m that circumstance unfortunately involved in his fate; for letters of M. Cazotte's were found in I. a Forte's possession, and the writer of them was sent to prison with his amiub e child. 'To Mademoiselle, in a few days liberty was offered ; but she refused it. and uhlan-' d permission to remain confined ; and it e affectionate zeal she testified for her father, united to the eloquent persuasions that sf>e used, so far interested the Marscllois (who were quartered m the prison) in his favor, that they unanimously determined to preset e (lis life. Though the ill fated old man's death was thus uncx|>ectedly prevented through lite filial attachment of his amiable child, vet his savage persecutors allowed him but a sin-it enjoyment of existence ; for on the evening of the 2d September. they again dimnnded his life. Mademoiselle Cazotte, htarmg i er father's name vociferated by voices wlt'ii

appalled every feeling by their sound, instantly rushed out amongst the gioup of murderers and undauntedly answered to the name. Her extreme youth, beauty, and courage, struck with astonishment the sanguinai y band ; and cruelty itsell remained some moment doubtful whether it should fulfil oppressive Tvrai r v's command. " What hast thou done to he I eie with thy daughter?" said one of the foremost to the ill fated Cazotte. " You will find tint by the jailor's book," replied the prisoner: which informed them, that, for fieing a couu. ter revolutionist, Cazotte was detained. Scarcely was the report circulated amoi g.«t them than the axe was raised over the unfortunate man's head ; which his daughter perceiving. uttered a shriek of hoiror, and throwing herself upon him concealed him from their sight. ' Strike barbarians said she, disdaining supplication; "for you cannot reach mv father, but through the passage of my heart !" At this astonishing proof of filial affection, beaits which had been strangers to eon. passion felt the force of Nature's ties ; a d a shout of I'ardon ; Pardon 1 issued from the mouths of the surrounding multitude, and was re echoed by ihe general voice. "1 be Marsellois instantly opened the passage for them, and the old man retired under the cover of his sacred shield !" What a tribute was at that moment offered to the social affections ! What transitions can exalted virtue produce in the heart ! Even barbarism itself seemed to acquire civilization ; ferocity became gentleness; aud

the oppressors were subdued I Afier the institution of the criminal tribunal Cazoite was again destined to feel the force of tyrannic power: again was he arrested and dragged to prison; and again, ia spit's of all entreaties, accompanied by his child. " in the company ofynu, my father," said tins amiable daughter, " the most cruel of aasas-

sins 1 have faced ; and shall ! not be the companion of your new misfortune, in which there is much less cause for dread or alarm. The hope of saving your life will again support me ; and 1 wilt show to your judges a forehead furrowed with age. 1 will ask them if a man, who has hut a few days to linger out among his fellow creatures, may not find mercy in the exes of justice, after having avoided the perils which you. have escaped ? J will inquire if him whose while hairs could excite pity in the breasts of assassins, could not create it in the hearts of magistrates, where mercy ought to reside ; The voice of Nature will plead and you will he liberated." " Oh !" said the unfortunate father, " deceive not yourself, my child ! Though i'atotte at length agreed that his daughter should accompany him to ptisou, yet the keeper positively refused to let her in; and agonized at this unexpected disappointment, she instantly flew to the commune, and by the foice of tears and supplications, at length had the satisfiction of obtaining consent. Night and day were spent in fihal affections, and in cndeavois to fortify h< r father's mind, except those hours when si e was trying to induce his judges to use their influence to preserve his life. When the period arrived which was to decide the destiny of the oppressed and unfortunate Cazolte, he appeared before the tribunal, supported by his amiable daughter, whose interesting appearar.ee excited genet al applause! Previous to that mock ceiemony

winch was falsely termed a trial, Cazotte had lain injunctions on his daughter not to speak ; but as they proceeded, the variations of her countenance expressed more than the most eloquent tongue could reveal. Breath less from fear, and pale from apprehension, in all the agony of suspense, she wailed to hi at the final sentence pronounced ; but, unable to support the dreadful conflict of feeling, she was carried apparently lifeless out of the hall ! The moment she had regained tiie powers cf recollection, she requested to be restored to that object whom nature had endeared ; but the tears ofiier friends too fatallv convinced her, she was never again destined to fie b est with his sight, for execution immediately followed the sentence, and it is to he hoped the unfortunate Cazotle was translated to a better life þÿ American Paper.
ON SEDUCTION. " Curse on that tongue, whose vile pernicious art, Delights the ear but to corrupt the heart."

What is seduction ? Reduction is a crime moulded in the blackest hvpocricv of a heart cruel and base, and brought forth by means equally vile and barbarous Seduction is a crime so much the more horrid, that it chooses its victims among the helpless and the weak. Women, gentle and sweet women, are the constant objects of its wretched pur suits, and not seldom fall an untimely prev to Us villainous perfidy. Seduction bewilders their susceptible minds in a romantic maze of visionary happiness, that it may the better throxv an insidious veil over the most sacred duties of their hearts; it dazzles them by the near and unnatural brilliancy of love's pictured aspects, that it ma v the better conceal from their view that wildness of shame and tniserv, whither its pcrfiduous hand leads thou incautious steps.

I. el a woman never expect happiness from a man who wants her to sacrifice honor and duty to his passions. He who wants te rob a woman of virtue, which makesnfl her strength, can be actuated but by the mean purpose of abusing her weakness By yielding to a man's unluwiul wishes, a woman renders herself despicable in his eyes ; thus she will soon lose her fascinating power þÿ thus the tie of love, so slender, when not strengthened i»y mutual esteem, will soon he broken, and ihe deluded victim he left to mount and to weep over her own infatuated credulity. A man, who trulv loves and esteems a woman. will think it turnout able to his sensibility, to pay her, on every occasion, that tribute of affectionate respect, width, of all created beings, women undoubtedly have the fairest claim to. But tl a man, in auiliessiug a wo man, shuns the lace of nay þÿ il lie ii.iks in the dark þÿ il he is afraid ol being seen, then let her beware of that man be is not a lover, tie is a villain, who meditates a lobbery, and plots a murdei ! Ynd more than a murdet ! for the dagger of die assassin could not i fl < t a deeper wound on a female's heatt, than even the whisper that can sully its | nitty and honour ' Woman is neiilict clothed in a tiger's skin, nor armed with a lion's stiengtti: the looks of meekness, the blushes ol modesty, the smiles of innocence, aim the fascination oi weakness united to beauty, uus only are the sacred thorns wnfi which kinduatuie has surrounded and guarded that beautiful rose. I bus de-

fenceless. women is. as n weie. thrown, by heaven itself, on man's genemsttv : then how base, how mean, how vile, must ihe seducer fie, when he betrays that honouratde and heavenly trust ! VY hen tie mocks die tender feelings of an helpless woman, whom naiuie iiisiiiictively leads to him as to her only protecmr. That feature alone renders die sedu cer infamous ; for, as in woman nothing can compensate for the absence of virtue, so, in man, nothing can atone for » tie w ant of honor. The seducer is a trai'or ; under the assumed garb of a true and pme affection, fie enters the temple, where innocent beauty dwells, and then, like a sacrilegious tofioer, violates its sanctuary, pollutes its al'ar, and plunders it of its riches. Vile reptile! he lurks under flowers, to allure an unsuspecting victim ; lie smooths the way he knows well will lead her to endless sorrow, to repentance. Remorseless wretch! he tears the dearest ties of affection and duty asunder; clouds the bright sun of domestic happiness, and chills friendship, even when it smiles on him Deaf to the feelings of nature, and the commanding voice of religion, the seducer overleaps their sacied barriers, and thus, traitor to humanity itself, he undermines, he subverts the noblest and surest basis of moral and social order. The seducer is equally cruel and ungrateful. He introduces moral turpitude in corporeal beauty; thus lie disoiders t fie noblest symmetry of the most elegant form. He debases woman, the fairest work of the Al-

mighty's hands ; he blasts that " plant of celestial seed," and nips it in its verv bud. He triumphs in rending wiih pangs of guilty remorse, a tender bosom, which sweet nature heaves in gentle signs of innocence and love. The seducer is born of a woman ; on a woman's breast his eyes shed their fust tears; from woman's breast his life drew its first support; and yet it is woman whom he persecutes, whom he betrays, whom he dooms to an unmerited misery to a lasting disgrace! þÿ Woman, whose devoted affection to man so

often outsteps the bounds of the strength and feeling of human nature. The seducer is a coward. The construction of tliose in the Belgium and the Rhenish provinces has thrown open to the travelling public, and made accessible at a moderate cost, the finest cities of the Netherlands, as well as the celebrated Banks of tire Rhine, and the scenery ot Switzerland. We are gratified in being enabled to supply the annexed description of this noble building to our readers, all the genera1 features of the structure being accurately described. When we consider the extent and character of this magnificent structure, and remember that the foundation stone was laid on ttie 7th of January, 1842, the completion of such a building, massive, beautiful, ami elaboraie beyond precedent in this country, we are struck wiiii admiration at the fact, that this monument of England's commercial greatness has been completed in less than three years. extent and site. To commence w ith the extent, the length of the edifice is about 300 feet from the east to west; or, accoiding to Mr. Tile's plan, 203 feci 0 inches from the columns of the portico, on the west, to the pilasters on the east, which we believe is the exact length. þÿ The general width of the building averages about 160 leet, the widih of the portico is 00 leet, and the extreme width at the east et.d, at the bioadest part, being 17b feet, and the width through the centre, from north to south, 144 feet. The site is so familiar to all partics, that, with reference the situation and to the surrounding objects, it will be sufficient to remark that the building, though not iectangulat, is regular. inscription on toe new rotai, exchange. On the aicliitrave of the north facade are three inscriptions insculpt in relief, each divided by a simple moulding. The one on the le it of the spectator is the common City

motto, " Domine, tnitige, nos," and that on the right is " honor, heo botii of which inscriptions every passer by, though unacquainted with Latin, can readily comprehend. Hot the motto in the central com pa 1 tmeut, " foktvn a. my," appears to puzzle thousands, and the Latin scholar more than any other þÿ Bv some it has been deciphered " Fortuna ait Muros" (prosperity to these walls) But the truth is, that it is not Latin, but Norman French, and was the motto of Sir Thomas Graham's family arms, Fortune amor (pros peritv to my house; or, literally, ' Fortune to me") In old Norman French the termination t or 01 is usually written y; the preposition a is not accented; and the omission ot the final e. in fortune (leaving it doubtful whether it is Latin or French) conduces to the general puzzle. þÿ Bells Weekly Messenger Oct: 28.

From the St. Thomas Times. Nov. 30, 1841. The It. M Gornpanv s'ennter Thames, arrived on Thursday morning from Jamaica, arid our files came to hand, but they are by no means interesting. 'J he House of Assembly is in session, and we observe that a bill has been introduced and read a second time to exempt vessels carrying the English mails from tonnage duties and fees, which if carried will be in our opinion a politic and wise enactment. We believe St. Thomas is the only port in the West Indies which has exhibited towards the Company a proper spirit of liberality, for here ! they enter and depart free of dues, and a light house lias been erected principally for their accommodalion in consequence of their arriving frequently during the night. The English islands ought in justice to the Company, which has made such large sacrifices to connect by means of steam, the Caribbean Archi,eiago with the old world, to abolish ail restrictions, impediments, and impositions. The company is by no means a legitimate object of taxation. The machinery of working it is costly, and hitherto not remuteiaive Its abandonment would be a seiious blew to the commercial community of this pait of the world. It should therefore be enc< uraged. It is a noble undertaking which confers lustre on the enterptise of the capitalists who undertook it. and we hope by the next steamer, that we shall hear of the bill having become law and trust, (of which there can be iit'ie doubt) that it will receive the Royal assent of the Queen of England. It may not be amiss to mention for the

information of our inn chants, that a quauuty of American goods have been seized and condemned in Kingston Jamaica ; by the officers of the Customs in consequence of lieing marked with English names purporting to he the names of manufacturers resident in the United Kingdom, ami that the same law is in force in all ihe British possessions, ntd came into operation on January 5. 1843. Such goods cannot be unpol led for exportation only, arid it is not necessary that the names brands or marks on the goods shall lc those ot some actually existing maiula< mrer in order to render tliem Jiatiie 10 seizure; it is sutiieieni that the maiks purport the goods to have been manufactured in Great Britain.

While the workpeople were engaged erecting the tent on the platform for Ins Majesty's reception they were startled bv cries of " Fire." and on turning towards the octagonal building they discovered the flames kindling in the upper part among the paint stores. A general alarm was instantly raised and, admission being obtained, the fire was found to have attained such a hold of the combustibles contained on 'he floors that it was impossible to prevent it from consuming

Ilis Majesty the King of the French arrived at the station about 11 o clock, and to get to the platform the royal carnage had to pass over several lengths of hose whilst the engines were at wot k. The scene at that moment was one of intense interest. The appearance of tire troops who formed the royal escort, the reflection of the flames upon their hi ight helmets and accoutrements, the roaring of the engines working, the shouting of tltc firemen, and the huzzas of the crowd in honour of the French Monarch, excited a feeling that can wi h difficulty he described. For some minutes the can iage remained stationary, and his Majesty viewed from the window the progress Ol the flames, which were within 100 feet ol him, the heat at that time being very great. The exact amount of property destroyed, and tlie extent of insurances, are as follows: I he octagonal building, as well as the fitting house, which was 120 feet long by U0 w ide, were insured in i he Westminster Eire Office tor 4000/., and the contents in the Phoenix Office to the amount ol 9000/., making a total of 13 000/. There were in the octagon six engines and three tenders, the foimer valued at 1300/. each, and the latter at 200/. each. It will cost an enormous sum to reinstate the machinery alone. The company estimate the damage under 20,000/. At first it was apprehended thai a sufficient number

of engines were not left for working the line, but we were assured that such was not tfie case, and the traffic will not he in the least retarded by the calamity. The cause of the lire has been traced to the spontaneous ignition of some vegetable black, which was stowed in the paint room.

There were, according to Mexican accounts, upward of four hundred Indians engaged in this. þÿ 'The atiair lasted over two hours, a lively fire being kept up all the while. '1 he Indians then abandoned the field, giving up the fifty five Mexicans, women and children, whom they had previouslv carried oil captives, a quantity of fire-arms, and some horses which they had stolen. 1 wenty of the Indians were left dead upon the field, while many more were believed to have been carried nil in the flight, according to Indian usage, both dead and wounded On the side of the Mexicans, nine were killed and thirty four wounded. The capture of the ship John N. Gossier by the Buenos Avrean squadron, and her subsequent release, have been mentioned. The particulars of that transaction are thus given in the journal do Commercio of liio de Janeiro: þÿ The John N. Gossier fell in with, off Montevideo, the Argentine sloop of war þÿ Twenty-fiih of May,' and was seized and brought to anchor outside the port under pretence that she had broken the blockade þÿ The supercargo, as soon as the vessel was anchored, went on board the American sloop of- war Boston,' lying in the harbor, which vessel sent an officer on board the Twentyfith of þÿMay, to inquire the cause of such detention. The answer returned by the commander was, that fie detained the ship because lie hud a right to do so.' The commander of the Boston' having received this answer, got under way aud anchoted close to the

'Twenty fith of þÿMay, and again sent a lieutenant on board the blockading vessel, and repeated the former question, and received the same answer as before. The lieutenant then said that hts commander did not recognize such a right, and demanded that an order be issued for the þÿvessel r s elease. The blockader refused to give such order. At other message was subsequently sent by the American commander, saying þÿ that if such an order was not sent to the vessel, he himself would give þÿit. The blockader again declared that he would not give such an order. Upon this, the þÿBoston again got under way, passed by the detained ship, and ordered her to weigh anchor and follow in her wake- -which she immediately did, and both vessels entered tlie hat bor. The American commander, it is understood, sent word to the blockading forces that he would not conseut ifuit an American vessel should be detained, impeded, or visited. The American consul on fns part said that the blockade existed only on paper, and was therefore not to be recognised þÿ þÿ Boston .Mercantile.
From Bells Weekly Messenger, London October 28. 1844. ANNIVERSARY OF l'HE BATTLE OF TRAFALGAR,

VISIT OF HKli MAJESTY TO THE VICTORY Among the memorable events by which the present month has been distinguished, and which will entitle it to a niche in 'the temple of fame, not the least interesting was tlie visit of our youthful Sovereign to the ship in which our great naval hero Nelson fought and died. 'The visit of her Majesty was made too, on Monday, the anniversary of the battle of T ralalgar. It appears that as her Majesty, with Prince Albeit, Lady Gainsborough, and Lord Liverpool, in the Koval barge, steered by Captain Bow lev, was making for the lloyn! Clarence Victualling Office, Portsmouth, through two lines of men of war barges, the extraoidinary denotations of the Victory attracted I er attention. Her Majesty inquired the reason of the crowning of the trucks of the toj masts with laurel, and the adornment of tlie figurehead, taflrail, decks, and sides, with the same evergreen; and on being informed by Captain Row ley that it was in consequence of that day being the anniversary of the battle of Trafalgar, her Majesty said, emphatically, þÿ I will go on board ihat ship;" and Captain Rowley immediately altered the course of the Royal barge, and steered alongside the Victory. This determination, as unexpected by those on board as it was to the Lords of the Admiralty, and ihe officers who were in their respective barges, took them ail bv surprise, arid when her Majesty went up the accommodation ladder Lieut. K. Jones (c). she second lieutenant ol the Victory, was the

only officer on deck to receive her Majesty, with Mr. Thomas, acting second master, and. Mr. R. B H. Ualdiffe, as side boys; Lieut. Smith fc), the very meritorious and observing first lieutenant, having been in the Admiralty barge as flag lieutenant, by special appointment, to the Lords of the Adniiialty, and Captain Moubray, in hi own tiaige, in the line of procession Her Majesty ttm handed up the side by Captain Rowley. «nd was followed by Prince Albert and her

þÿMajesty suite. s Captain Kowley, with Mr. A leh. the master, conducted her Majesty to the quarter deck, and. by special desire, to the spot where Nelson received his death wound. Never since the day on which the immortal Nelson fell has the anwiveisarv of that victory been celebrated with a mote interest i nsr or becoming tribute of affection and respect than when our beloved Monarch stood upon the quarter deck of the deceased hero's favourite ship, and shed a tear upon the spot where he ended his gallant career. The 21st of October has ever been held sacred to his memory, but not even Nelson's lamented death, nor the glorious triumph with which it was accompanied, will he mote sacred than the remembrance of that exoui site feeling of patriotism evinced by her Majesty on reading aloud the affecting inscription þÿ þÿ Here Nelson þÿfell. The Queen of England plucked from the wreath of laurel in which it was enshrined two of its leaves, and carefully treasured them as a precious memento of the departed hero. Her Majesty then went over to the poop rail, where, over the steering wheel, is inscribed in letters of gold the words of the memorable signal, " England expectseverv man will do his duty." '1 his inscription was also adorned with laurels and flowers. With marked emphasis her iMajest v repeated the words ; and on an explanation by Captain Kowley as to the signal of the immortal hero, and its enthusiastic reception by the fleet, her Majesty attempted to pluck another leaf to add to the

?toie of her remembrance. Conducted bv Mr. V i len, her Majesty then descended to he lower decks. On passing from the main deck, which was in great confusion from »he recent salute which tiad been fired, a powder monkey, wiih iittle ceremony in gnornnee of the quality of the visitors, ran against the Queen while bringing up a fresh supply of powder. Her Majesty was staggered, but was in no wav displeased, and made light of the concussion. The cockpit was entered, her Majesty observing tbit the height of the orlop desk was not so great as in other ships she had visited. The Royal party proceeded to the cabin, in which the very spot hallowed by the termination of Nelson's glorious earthly career is marked by a funeral urn (in paint), surmounted by Nelþÿson f s lag, and on its top, encircled in a wreath, me words, þÿ Here Nelson þÿdied. There was a pause here for several minutes. and it was remarked that her Majesty was again much affected by the reflections which such a scene awakened.
